objection.original: sed nos nullum angelum audimus contra Paulum apostolum

objection.original: festinat patrem ante intercipere quam occidere
objection.english: he hurries to catch his father before he kills him
objection.explain: [8] Intercipere here means 'kill': he wants his father dead before he has killed him, repeating the preceding paradox of impatient haste.

objection.explain: In [6] and [7], both present participles mean 'changing into fiery heat', not 'having changed into it'; this repeated aspect shift replaces ongoing change with completion, the distinction expressly under discussion.

objection.original: quasi obsoleta corporatos communione
objection.english: as if they were incorporated in an outworn communion
objection.explain: Here obsoleta means sullied or polluted: the accusation concerns a tainted communion, not an outdated one.

fixed.work: Libellus Adversus eos qui contra Synodum Scribere Praesumpserunt

fixed.before: "Whoever you are who judge, in that in which you judge another you condemn yourself: for you who judge do the same things. And we know that the judgement of God is according to truth against those who do such things; and again: Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. What evil reasoning is this, that one who steals should preach that one must not steal, and should clothe a brow prodigal of shame in the cloud of attacking another? No one rightly takes on the part of an admonisher unless he condemns errors by his own acts and shows a love of innocence in his way of life. For even tax-collectors can condemn in speech the vices dear to their own habits, and by the more wicked offices of the tongue punish what they love, as if it were not a kind of greater excess to give with the lips affection to a thing you despise in your mind, and to clothe the venom of your character in the honey of conversation. I act in this way as if you had shame, chastity, grace of feeling, or as if anyone were allowed to accuse a teacher and fit the bites of a livid mouth against one who is elect, when beforehand, foreknowing what was to come, I had warned you with full voice in the letter given to you: Who shall bring accusation against the elect of God? It is God who justifies: who is he that condemns? And again: O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, do you think that you will escape the judgement of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering? You accuse wickedness, being filled with iniquity, fornication, avarice, malice, envy, murders, condemnation, deceit, malignity, proud, arrogant, inventors of evils, disobedient to a parent, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy. objection.original: I ei quid est pietatis in reliquum
objection.english: whatever affection remains to her
objection.explain: Reading the evident corruption as si quid, this means 'if any dutiful affection remains'; it does not attribute the remaining affection to Rome.

fixed.work: Libellus Adversus eos qui contra Synodum Scribere Praesumpserunt
fixed.author: Ennodius, Magnus Felix
fixed.before: After this, if you grow sicker under the doctors' treatment and no regard for your salvation brings you back from what you have begun, at least look to your city, the parent of the world: she herself, after her defenders the apostles, approaches you mourning; she herself addresses you and, whatever affection remains to her, begins a speech that will win its plea:
fixed.after: After this, if you grow sicker under the doctors' treatment and no regard for your salvation brings you back from what you have begun, at least look to your city, the parent of the world: she herself, after her defenders the apostles, approaches you mourning; she herself addresses you and, if any dutiful affection remains [in you], begins a speech that will win its plea:
fixed.reason: The scan's 'I ei quid' is evidently 'si quid': Rome speaks to them 'if any dutiful affection remains' in them, not 'whatever affection remains to her'.

objection.original: quod mundo studetis me uenerabiles
objection.english: that you, my venerable ones, are zealous for the world
objection.explain: With apparent OCR me for esse, the sense is 'that you strive to be held in honour by the world', not that you are devoted to the world; venerabiles is predicative, not a vocative.

fixed.work: Libellus Adversus eos qui contra Synodum Scribere Praesumpserunt
fixed.author: Ennodius, Magnus Felix
fixed.before: "Behold me, made conspicuous, whom the temples of the most high God made to rejoice in the splendour of a new light, once the worship of the shrines was repudiated; me, whom, after filthy chapels polluted with much gore of cattle, the outpouring of the Lord's and the apostles' blood cleansed from the blood of victims; me, whom health, restored after long fevers, made despise the sanctuaries; me, whom the offering freed from victims; I who acquired the peace of Christ through enmity with idols; I, to whom gifts were hardly more numerous than gods; me, whom my religion made a beggar through its varied devotions; me, whom poverty had crushed as I constantly asked favours of my gods; I who sent to Tartarus the Curii, the Torquati, the Camilli, whom the church did not regenerate, and the rest, an unfruitful mother of a most numerous offspring, while I wasted away, ill delivered, with my womb exhausted; because the saving of their country did not redeem the Fabii, and the glory won with much sweat availed the Decii nothing. Innocence of works without faith was ruined: Scipio, most observant of justice, was joined to the criminal, because he did not know Christ. I would wish to draw my pen through the whole of my infancy, if the breast of a bereaved woman could bear it. But whoever rereads past things worthy of lamentation seems to desire times of tears. No one is believed to have grieved over those whose recounting does not wound him: he who keeps a dry face while recounting the deaths of his children is convicted of cruelty by a sure witness. Behold, now in that sanctuary of liberty nothing servile is found from the worship of idols; behold, the crown of honours, the genius of the world, the Roman flower, tramples in full sanctity the altars it long venerated; behold, now my senate house is called to heaven, praised, received, and I cannot say that after the grace of baptism I have lost any offspring, even one that sudden death took away. The supreme Ruler embraces many holders of the trabea and the curule chair without loss of their dress or dignity; now the munificence of an earthly triumph almost purchases divine favour, and this profits for the grace of Christ, that you, my venerable ones, are zealous for the world. Behold, now the wet thresholds send candidates to the portable chair of the apostolic confession, and with abundant tears, joy exacting them, the gifts conferred by God's kindness are doubled."

objection.original: quibus est quidem inedium, sed caret nomine
objection.english: those which have a mean indeed, but lack a name
objection.explain: The unnamed thing is the intermediate, not the contraries: 'those which have an intermediate that lacks a name'.

fixed.author: Augustine, Saint
fixed.before: There are four species of opposites: for one thing is opposed to another, first, either in the form of the category which is called relation; second, or in the manner of contraries; third, or of those concerning which a having or a privation is said to be about us (here indeed we should take 'having' from the verb 'to have', not, as we defined above, that a state is a certain lasting disposition of the mind); in the fourth way, when we either affirm or deny something: for example, let us set out an example from those that are called relatives. The first [kind of] opposite appears [as] the double to the single, or a father to a son. Let the second, the example of contraries, be bad to good. The third, of those that are spoken of by having and privation, as blindness and sight. The fourth, of those in which there is negation and affirmation, as 'he runs', 'he does not run'. The distinction between contraries and relatives is evident to those who consider [it]: for things called relatives are named from what is opposed to them; for the single is the opposite of the double, and the double the opposite of the single: but contraries have what they are called from themselves, and do not need another. For who would say 'the bad of the good', or who 'the good of the bad'? This, then, is the lucid and clear distinction between these two species which come from opposites. Contraries themselves are divided into three species: for either they have a mean, that is, they have something between them; or they are without a mean; or, as reason has found in certain cases, they have a mean indeed, but its name does not appear, unless it is made up from the negation of each opposite. Those with a mean, then, are these, white and black, between which, since pale or dusky can arise, these opposites are called mediated. In those that are mediated, it is not necessary that one of the two opposites be found in a body: for if it is not black, it can be dusky; or if white is lacking, pale can be found. But of those opposites which are not mediated, one of the two must necessarily occur, as is health and sickness. Of these there is no mean, because human bodies must necessarily hold either health or sickness. But those which have a mean indeed, but lack a name unless it is formed from the negation of the opposites, are these, just and unjust: there is something in the middle, but it has no name; and so the negation of each opposite creates a name for it, so that we call that which is in the middle neither just nor unjust. Now let us go over more carefully those opposites which arise through having and privation: for in these it must be observed that both are in the same matter, in the same place, at the proper time. Blindness and sight are in the same matter; for they consist in seeing and not seeing. They are also in the same place; for both blindness and sight have their place in the eyes. Most of all, however, the fitness of the time is required in these: for no one is rightly called bald unless at the time when he ought to have hair he does not have it: nor can anyone call toothless, whom the Greeks call *nōdos*, an infant to whom tender age has so far denied teeth. For privation, which in Greek is called *sterēsis*, has this force, that it shows that someone had something by nature and does not have it. Among these things we should remember that it is one thing to be sight and blindness, another to have sight and to be deprived of it; lest, if we judge these to be the same, the reasoning should seem confused. But if anyone thinks this doubtful or too little certain, let him notice what follows each thing. For if the blind and blindness were the same, both would be said of one [thing]: but we say a man is blind; yet a man cannot be called blindness: it is clear, therefore, that it is one thing to be blind, another to be blindness. Nor are affirmation and negation the same as the things that fall under affirmation and negation. Yet all are likewise held to be opposed to one another. Sometimes, however, evils are opposed to evils, whenever the means between contraries are good, as is deficiency and excess, which the Greeks call *endeia kai hyperbolē*. For between these two evils opposed to each other, moderation is sought as the mean. Following this reasoning the Peripatetics said that the virtues are means, so that they called more than is just *pleonexia*, less than is just *meionexia*: between which evils they placed justice in the middle. Similarly, between cunning and dullness they placed prudence; between lust and insensibility, which the Greeks call *anaisthēsia*, temperance is set; between timidity and rashness, courage. Thus reason, searching thoroughly, has found a certain hidden kind of opposites, so that sometimes evils are found to be contrary to evils. But Aristotle explained more fully and in many ways the properties and differences of these four species which come from opposites: for us, however, let it suffice to have set out both genus and species, lest, occupied with minuter matters, we wear down the necessary ones with tedium.

objection.original: ὀλιγίστων δὲ φλέβα τεμεῖν ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς νόσου τολμησάντων ἐνίων ἰατρῶν
objection.english: When a very few of the physicians dared to open a vein at the beginning of the disease
objection.explain: The very few are the patients whose veins were opened: 'Some physicians dared to bleed very few patients at the beginning of the disease.'

fixed.author: Galen
fixed.before: The famines that have occurred continually, for not a few years in succession, among many of the peoples subject to the Romans have clearly shown, to those at least who are not wholly senseless, how great a power bad humour has for the generation of diseases. For the city-dwellers, as was their custom to lay in at once during the summer enough grain for the whole following year, took all the wheat from the fields, together with the barley, the beans and the lentils, and left to the country people the other fruits of Demeter, which they call pulses and legumes, while also carrying not a few even of these into the town. So the people in the countryside, having used up what was left during the winter, were forced to use foods producing bad humour throughout the whole spring, eating shoots and sprouts of trees and shrubs, and bulbs, and roots of plants with bad humours, and stuffing themselves too with the so-called wild greens, whatever anyone happened to have plenty of, unsparingly, to the point of surfeit, just as they also boiled and ate whole green herbs which they had never before tasted even by way of trial. One could therefore see some of them at the end of spring, and almost all at the beginning of summer, seized by very many sores forming on the skin, which did not have the same form in all; for some of them were erysipelatous, some inflammatory, some spreading, some lichen-like, and itch-like, and leprous. Of these, the mildest, breaking out through the skin, evacuated the bad humour from the viscera and the depths; but in some people, becoming carbuncular and phagedenic [i.e. eating away the flesh], accompanied by fevers, they killed many over a long time, with scarcely a very few saved. And apart from the affections of the skin there were very many fevers, bringing on foul-smelling and biting evacuations of the bowel, ending in tenesmus and dysenteries, and acrid urine, itself also foul-smelling, which ulcerated the bladder of some. Some of them reached a crisis through sweats, these too foul-smelling, or through putrid abscesses. Those in whom none of these occurred all died, either with evident inflammation of at least one of the viscera, or because of the severity and malignancy of the fevers. When a very few of the physicians dared to open a vein at the beginning of the disease (for they were reasonably afraid to use this remedy, because the strength had already been broken down beforehand), I saw in no one good blood drawn off, such as is seen being evacuated from healthy bodies, but either redder, or blacker, or more serous, or acrid and biting the very vein that had been cut as it flowed out, so that the wound became hard to heal. In some, and especially in those who died, there also occurred with the fevers symptoms bringing on damage to the mind, with sleeplessness and lethargic stupor. It is nothing surprising that those who fell ill at that time were seized by opposite diseases and symptoms, since they differed from one another not only in their natures or their ages, but also in their previous regimens, and had eaten during the famine foods having opposite powers. For all ate whatever they had plenty of; but since the supply was unequal, some took foods having sour, or acrid, or salty, or bitter juices, others astringent, or harsh, or clearly cooling, or very moist, or sticky, or drug-like. I know, at any rate, some who died at once from eating mushrooms, some from hemlock or giant fennel, and not a few of them who were scarcely saved. Now to all other people who considered it with reason it appeared clearly that, just as on the outside there occurred ulcerations of many kinds and various sorts of swellings, inflammatory and oedematous, erysipelatous and scirrhous, so also in some of the parts in the depths, those that are more vital, just as many conditions could have arisen. Only in those who have departed from Hippocrates' teaching about the humours was reason maimed, as they venture to blame everything rather than the humours. Some of them admitted to me privately that they clearly saw the contentiousness against Hippocrates of those who think that nothing either good or bad, even towards disease, comes from humours, but that they were ashamed to go over to Hippocrates after fifty years of age; for in this way, they said, they would seem to have harmed not only their pupils but also those who had employed them during all the previous time. And indeed they said that they were already honoured by many people, as [holding] true the doctrines they championed; but if they admitted that these too were bad, they would appear more ignorant than the others, and none of those who had previously employed them would ever employ them again. To these, then, it is reasonable for us to grant much indulgence, not blaming their choice, but sharing their grief at their misfortune, since before they were able to judge what was taught they fell in with teachers who were not good. But worthy of hatred are those who first, out of ambition, set up sects of doctrines; for they evidently attempted willingly to deceive their neighbours, not erred unwillingly, since no human being has come to such folly as not to know how great an evil it is for the humours in the body to be turned to drug-like qualities. At any rate these very people, against whom the argument is directed, say that it is difficult or even utterly impossible to distinguish those who perish from taking deadly drugs from those [who perish] from a morbid condition of the body itself. Yet no one can deny that we clearly see the juices of the so-called venomous beasts, which they inject through the bite, some of them quickly mortifying the bitten part, some also putrefying it, or bringing on inflammations or very great pains; just as [no one can deny] that someone fasting who spits two or three times on a scorpion at once kills the creature. For just as some natures are akin to [other] natures, so others are hostile and destructive to others. So it happens that we are nourished by what is akin, and destroyed by what is opposite. This has been discussed at great length both in the treatises On the Natural Faculties and in those On Simple Drugs; but for the present discussion the account of what was seen in the famines is sufficient. If you are willing to believe me, who have no reason to lie, but am vexed that many men in books have lied greatly, I shall relate to you what I have learned by long experience through my whole life, calling the gods also to witness. I had a father who had reached the summit in geometry and architecture, in calculation and arithmetic and astronomy, and who was admired by all who knew him for justice, goodness and self-control, as none of the philosophers [was]. He, then, regulating my regimen himself when I was a boy, kept me free of disease. But when I became a youth, and my father had withdrawn to the country, being fond of farming, I clung to my studies beyond all my fellow students, not only by day but also by night; and having stuffed myself, along with those of my age, throughout the whole fruit season with all the seasonal fruits, I fell ill in autumn with an acute disease, so that I needed venesection. From then on, sometimes in each successive year, sometimes skipping one year, I fell ill until twenty-eight years of age. At that point, having been in danger of getting an abscess in the part where the liver joins the diaphragm, I determined to abstain from all seasonal fruits except figs and grapes that were perfectly ripe, and even these I took not immoderately, as before, but in moderation. So, attending to exercise and to never suffering indigestion, we have remained free of disease up to now for many years; and of my other friends, as many as I persuaded to exercise and to live by an ordered regimen, I see all of them to this day continually in health, some for twenty-five years, others for fewer, but already a good number, according as each happened to be persuaded to abstain from the seasonal fruits and from the other foods producing bad humour, which it is proposed to go through in this treatise.

objection.original: mediante septimana quadragesimae sanctorum jejuniorum
objection.english: in the middle week of the forty days of the holy fasts
objection.explain: Mediante septimana means midway through the week during Lent, not during the middle week of Lent.

fixed.author: Dionysius Exiguus
fixed.before: There appeared, he says, the thrice most blessed and universal apostle and faithful friend of our Saviour Jesus Christ, in the middle week of the forty days of the holy fasts, on the eighteenth day of the month Peritius, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the seven hundred and sixty-third year, in the sixth indiction, in the reign of Valentinian and Marcian, most pious emperors and servants of God, under Uranius, most holy bishop of the city of Emesa, to whom this same thing was also revealed on the twenty-fourth day of the same month, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of March. And he revealed [it] to me, Marcellus, who was in great fear and reverence, in the form of a fiery star, according to the most trustworthy visions set out below: he who founded all things in his power and prepared [them] in his wisdom; who knows all things before they come to be, and orders everything for the salvation of the human race; who is blessed above all for ever. Amen. So God deigned to make me, his servant, the beholder of the vision set forth. For I saw in a vision of the night, and behold, the doors of our monastery were open, and, seized with great fear, I ran to shut them. And again I see a river bursting out at our doors. When I had seen this, I wondered in amazement where so vast a mass of water came from. And while I was turning this over within myself, raising my eyes I saw Marcellus the presbyter, who was second after Maxentius the archimandrite, coming from the southern side of the river, and we heard the voices of many companies from the eastern quarter of the basilica of the holy martyr Julian. A great sound of them was carried to us, and the peoples were hurrying through the waters themselves with eager rush. And as I marvelled how, walking in the midst of the waters, they came swiftly to us, and how each company chanted psalms in its own tongue, suddenly a voice was heard of those who were crying out from the east: 'Behold, Saint John the Baptist is coming down.' And while I was standing at the southern door, the eastern gates were opened, and the companies of psalm-singers came straight in. So leaving the sight of the river, and standing at the foot of the stairs, I watched their holy office, which they were celebrating in the monastery. And standing on the same stairs, I saw two courts, one facing west and the other south; and between the two courts a great temple, and each company entered the court that faced east, and worshipped toward the temple. But entering the southern court, they at once fell quiet. And when the companies had fallen silent, others went ahead and cried out: 'Behold, Saint John is coming.' And while I was standing at the same place on the stairs, Saint John, the forerunner of the Lord, came, and I saw him in the temple that had been shown to me; and behold, there was one at his right and one at his left. And as he stood in the temple, the peoples of the companies began to approach him one after another and to be blessed by him; and likewise, chanting psalms, they set off for the basilica of the holy martyr Stephen. And when the companies had passed through, I too thought to go to him, to be blessed by him. And it seemed good to me to go in by those doors by which the companies had entered. And since I had not seen that they gave anyone the kiss of peace, but only that they kissed his feet, approaching him from the front with fear and reverence, I ran with my head bowed to the ground and held his feet. But he took hold of my chin and kissed me. When I had been granted this, I at once awoke. And after a few days had passed, I see, and behold, the doors of the monastery on the southern side were open again, and I was shouting, as it were, at the brothers why they had left those doors [open]; and I went with quick step to shut them, and behold, I see Saint John standing at the outer door, and with him those two whom I had seen before, and I went up to be blessed by him, and raising me up again, he gave me peace. His garments were white; and presently drawing from his bosom a vessel full of honey, he gave [it] to me, saying: 'Receive this blessing,' and he poured that vessel of honey over my hands, and I asked him, saying: 'Lord Saint John, where have you come to us from?' He answered: 'I have come from Sebaste.' So I went before him, and both he and those who were with him entered our monastery, and again he poured the vessel of honey over my hands. And when I had carried his blessing to the upper part of the dining-hall, he entered the oratory; and when I had gone down to the oratory where he was, behold, I see a pillar of fire before him. And seized with great dread, I was woken. After this, before the door of the monastery where the holy deposit was had been handed over to us, in the holy days of the fasts, when we had taken food in the evening, I said to our brothers, 'Let none of you neglect to repeat his psalms.' And leaving me in the dining-hall, they went down to the foot of the stairs that looks toward both monasteries. And when they had sat down to repeat the psalms, Brother Isaac, raising his eyes to the right, saw fire burning on the panels of the door of the cave where the venerable head of Saint John the Baptist had been laid away. When the brother saw this, he cried out and said: 'My lord, my lord, a fire has been kindled at the door of the cave.' And I answered: 'Do not be afraid, brother, but, guarding yourself with the sign of Christ, stay right there.' But the brothers, shutting the door out of fear, came hurrying to me. I, however, recognising the mystery from the visions shown to me before, said to them: 'Do not be afraid, my brothers, for the Lord will make this turn out well for us.' And after five days Maxentius and Stephen, venerable presbyters and archimandrites, coming to the holy bishop on the Lord's day in the evening, put to him everything about that cave, which adjoined our monastery, so that both might be joined together; and the bishop ordered this to be done. The presbyter Stephen said to him: 'By our order I will hand the cave over to Brother Marcellus early tomorrow.' And arriving in the morning he handed that monastery over to us in the presence of the presbyters Palladius, Peter, Gennadius, and Stephen, archimandrite of the monastery of the Bethgali. And opening the door that was barred, we went in together and worshipped. And seeing that the place was very much neglected, he urged us to take care of it. And that same presbyter Stephen set out to visit the monasteries that were situated in the hamlets. I, Marcellus, taking the brothers, began to devote care to the monastery that had been given to us. And while we were cleaning those places, Peter, presbyter of the place Bethmamas, came and said to me: 'Stephen, archimandrite of the Bethgali, begs that for the Lord's sake you come with us to the monastery of blessed Carterius.' And I answered that I could not come, because I was devoting care to the place entrusted to me; but he compelled me to set out with him. And as we were going along together, I say to him: 'Let us go up and greet Cyriacus, deacon and archimandrite.' And going up and greeting him, we began to want to go on to the aforesaid monastery of blessed Carterius. And the deacon Cyriacus said to me: 'Did you come for this, to leave without delay?' I answered him: 'We must travel quickly, because another monastery has also been handed over to us by the bishop, to which we are urgently devoting care.' So going down we came to the monastery often mentioned; and when we had greeted the brothers and arranged what was necessary, we were returning. The aforesaid Peter and Stephen, presbyters and archimandrites, say to me: 'We bid you farewell; pray for us.' Then I say to them: 'Today we have taken over the monastery, and you want to go away? Stay, I beg you, and comfort us'; and I prevailed on them. And when evening had come, after prayers, having taken food, we went to rest: both of them in the upper dining-hall, I there in the inner chamber.

Stay, I beg you, and comfort us'; and I prevailed on them. And when evening had come, after prayers, having taken food, we went to rest: both of them in the upper dining-hall, I there in the inner chamber.

objection.original: et excusatum est illi

objection.original: tuis assistat altaribus
objection.english: this handmaid of yours too stands at your altars
objection.explain: Assistat continues the prayer as a wish: 'may this handmaid of yours too stand at your altars', rather than asserting that she stands there.

fixed.work: De Institutione Virginis Et Sanctae Mariae Virginitate Perpetua
fixed.author: Ambrose, Saint, Bishop of Milan
fixed.before: 108. Look therefore, Father, upon your gift, for whose sanctifying you sought no one's counsel; but without any suitor or arbiter you conferred on her so great a grace as no one could have believed before the divine oracles: that a virgin should carry God in her womb. Stirred by the privilege of this gift, the pursuits of virginity and the examples of sacred integrity multiply. Provoked by these to the grace of such virtue, this handmaid of yours too stands at your altars, not bringing golden hair from glowing locks devoted to the bridal veil, but that hair with which that woman of the Gospel, holy Mary, wiped the feet of Christ with diligent devotion and filled the whole house with the poured-out ointment, offering it to be consecrated by the sacred veil (John 12:3).

objection.english: he might reasonably be thought to have been given
objection.explain: In [1], δεδωκέναι is active: 'might reasonably be thought to have given'; the English reverses the giver and recipient.

fixed.author: Libanius
fixed.before: So the man who has made sure that what he would have lost, had he not obtained this last thing, will remain securely his, how could he not have robbed us of many places and many positions? objection.original: ne non esset suum quod evitaret peccatum
objection.english: lest the sin he was to avoid should not be his own
objection.explain: In [18], what is his own is the act of avoiding sin: 'lest his avoidance of sin not be his own act'; the Latin does not attribute ownership of the sin.

fixed.author: Isidorus Hispalensis
fixed.before: The human being was entrusted to the freedom of his own choice at once in his first condition, so that, by the vigilance of the mind alone exerting itself, he would also persevere in keeping the commandment, if he wished to remain in that state in which he had been created. But after he fell through Eve by the seduction of the serpent, he lost the good of nature, and likewise the vigour of choice; not, however, the power of election, lest the sin he was to avoid should not be his own, and lest what he had not washed away by choice should be pardoned without merit. Therefore freedom of choice, that is, rational will, remains for seeking salvation, but with God first admonishing and inviting to salvation, so that it may choose, or follow, or act upon the occasion of salvation, that is, upon the inspiration of God. But that it attains what it chooses, or what it follows, or what it does upon the occasion, we freely confess to be of God. So we have the beginning of our salvation by God's mercy; that we assent to the saving inspiration is within our power; that we obtain what we desire by assenting to the admonition is of divine gift; that we do not fall away from the gift of salvation once obtained is a matter of our own care and likewise of heavenly help; that we fall away is within our power and of our sloth. Not, however, for obtaining [salvation] without him who makes seekers find, who opens to those who knock, who gives to those who ask. So, just as we believe that we have the beginning of our salvation with God showing mercy and inspiring, so we freely confess that the choice of our nature follows divine inspiration. Therefore, that we do not fall away from the good either of nature or of merit is a matter of our own care and likewise of heavenly help; that we fall away is within our power and of our sloth.

objection.original: ex quolibet vasorum suorum
objection.english: from each of his jars
objection.explain: Quolibet means any one of the jars: he orders one flask filled from any jar, not from each jar.

fixed.before: There is said to be a certain man, Donatus, father of a son who was also most honourable, named Rusticus, an accountant of the prefects, very well known to all. On his suburban estate, called by the name of its place, he used to lay down and keep wines of good quality every year. Meanwhile, as is the custom of landowners, for the sake of profitable gain, to prefer to offer whatever produce of the land they have stored for sale to buyers at the moment when the prices of the season run higher, in line with their wishes for the profits they long for, it seemed good to the said master of the estate to go first into his wine-store with a certain man of his, a most expert taster of wine, and to approve the wines by examining them jar by jar. When this was done, as soon as the taster put the wine drawn from a jar to the judgement of his lips, at once the man's astonished mouth and face turned pale. For besides the fact that the wine's most foul colour offered of itself a sight for the eyes to turn from, its most dismal savour also forced on the lips a taste to grieve at. But since this evil was thought to lie in one jar only, the loss was not held to be so troublesome a damage to the householder. But when they began to go round jar by jar, and the whole number of the jars, that is, nearly two hundred, was examined and found to have likewise degenerated and perished, what the owner's feelings were there at that moment, what the grief of the store-keeper himself, I think no compassionate human heart can fail to know. For indeed no small and contemptible loss or damage had befallen, but nearly two hundred jars, as I said, which were thought to be completely full of the sweetest wine, were on the contrary found filled with the filth not even of vinegar, but of some most corrupt and dreg-laden liquid. What was the master of his ruined property to do, having suffered the destruction of his vintage not still on the vines, but, what is more grievous, in the wine-store itself? What, I say, was he to do? What could he have done with wine so corrupt and no longer to be called wine? Should he perhaps have sold it at some utterly worthless price? But what buyer would be so foolish as to approach so worthless a thing? Should he at least pour it out and throw it away? But who would so forget his own labours as readily to expose the produce of a whole year, such as it was, to be trampled by men and beasts? At last his soul, tossing in such griefs, breathed upon by the breeze of divine inspiration, was brought by grace, as by sail, into the most faithful harbour and the safest anchorage. For as he turned many things over within himself, this better resolve settled in the owner's mind: that he must take refuge with the Friend of God, Saint Stephen, the first martyr of Christ. So he ordered that taster of his wine to fill one small flask from each of his jars, to carry it at dawn to the shrine of the Blessed one to be blessed, and from there at once to bring it back sanctified, and then to pour a little of it over into all the jars and go away. So that faithful servant quickly carried out his master's orders: he drew the flagon as he had been told, went, set it down, brought it back, gave a very little to each jar, and went away. On the next day, mindful of his faith and of his order, the householder rose early, met the servant who knew of the task, and led him along with him as his companion to the wine-store: all the jars are inspected again in order; the wine is drawn, brightness is seen in the colour, the savour is approved in the taste, sadness is changed into joy, and it is found how much and how greatly faith in Christ and in his most glorious Friend avails, and the news passes on to all who hear and marvel; finally, those most excellent wines are distributed to buyers at a fitting price. See how divine providence serves the needs of men: and what, then, is offered or rendered to God for such great benefits of his?

objection.original: nativitatem ejus a secundo Abra- hae Dominus in Isaac semine spopondit atque pol- licitus est
objection.english: the Lord pledged and promised his birth from the second Abraham in the seed of Isaac
objection.explain: The a is a footnote marker; secundo means a second time and Abrahae means to Abraham: the Lord again promised Abraham his birth in Isaac's seed.

fixed.author: Bachiarius Monachus
fixed.before: 7. Do not spurn, I beg you, a dead brother: he is the son of the barren Shunammite woman (2 Kgs. 4:20), that is, of the Church; he who has died was born by promise. For long ago the Lord pledged and promised his birth from the second Abraham in the seed of Isaac (Gen. 22:15; Heb. 11:18). His head was struck by the heat at harvest, that is, the ruling part of his mind grew hot in the very flame of lust. Let his mother run to Elisha, that is, let the Church lament with anxious care: for he will rise again, if we hope for this faithfully from Christ. And you, most blessed one, imitate Elisha's work on your dead brother: lay hands on hands, feet on feet, mouth on mouth. First, so that you may suffer with him who lies dead, and not, exalted by the triumph of your own integrity, tower over him or stretch yourself above him whom sudden death has seized; but imitate the Apostle, who says: I fear lest my Lord God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who sinned before (2 Cor. 12:21). Then set your eyes upon his eyes, so that they may no longer wander off to his ruin; [your mouth] upon his mouth, so that it may not speak wicked things; [your hands] upon his hands, so that they may not do hostile things; [your feet] upon his feet, so that they may not wander in shameful ways. And so, when your limbs have been joined to his limbs to guard him, not only will he have no further room to sin, but he will also take hope of rising again; so that he who died from the cold of sin may be called back to life by the warmth of consolation. For a very secret and solitary place must be prepared for a man dead in sins, where nothing more is contained than the physician and the corpse.

fixed.author: SS Felix I

We exhort you, brethren (James I), to bear persecutions and tribulations patiently, so that you may be found sons of him whom daily you call Father, God in heaven; and that you may overcome all things in him who overcame all things for our sake: who also did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all (Romans VIII). It is fitting too that imitators of God imitate God in every word and deed (Maximus of Aquileia, session 4 of the same Lateran Council held in the year 649). And therefore we ought to say what the Lord himself declared of himself: The prince of this world will come, and will find nothing in me (John XIV). Those too have come who persecute you and us, for they cannot persecute you without us, since we are members of the one God, and through his sanctification we hold his one priesthood, and they have found nothing of their own in us: for whatever we are, we are by the grace of God, although for that reason they have striven irrationally to slander us, as enemies are wont to do, hastening thereby to cover up their own madness, so that by falsehood they may be able to overshadow the truth. For I have written to you, says the blessed apostle, with many tears, not that you should be saddened, but that you may know what charity I have more abundantly towards you (II Corinthians II). For to disparage those who disparage (Deusdedit, bishop of Cagliari, in the same place) is not good, lest, roused by the things that have been written, we make a contest of injury. We ought not at all to fear the reproach of men (Martin I, session 3 in the same place), nor to be overcome by their reproaches, since the Lord commands us this through the prophet Isaiah, saying: Hear me, you who know judgement, my people, in whose hearts is my law (Isaiah LI). Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies (Psalm XLIII). Considering also what is written in the psalm: Will not God search out these things? For he knows the secrets of the heart, and the thoughts of such men, that they are vain. And each one has spoken vain things to his neighbour, deceitful lips [are] in the heart, and with the heart they have spoken evil things. But the Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. They have said: Our lips are our own; who is our lord (Psalm XI)? For if they kept these things in memory, they would by no means leap forth into such great iniquity. For (the words of the same pope) they do this not through approved and fatherly teaching, but in order to exercise their vengeance on the servants of God. For it is written: The way of the fool is right in his own eyes. And there are ways which seem just to a man, but their end leads to death (Proverbs XII, XIV). For we who suffer these things ought to reserve them to the judgement of God (Third Roman Council, under Symmachus), who will render to each according to his works (Jeremiah XV). For in this dwelling the Lord promised blessing and eternal life. Embracing, therefore, the merit of this prophetic utterance, we have set out the present brotherly letter, seeking, and intending to seek, by no means our own things, for charity's sake. For it is not good to disparage those who disparage, or, according to the common saying, to knock out a stake with a stake. Far be it. These things are not ours: wherefore may the Godhead turn them away. Our habits have not been taught to conquer in this way, but in the patience of long-suffering and in the spirit of humility: for just as fennel-flower (to speak prophetically) is by no means cleaned by hardness (Daniel III), so neither is the restful fruit of peace and understanding pressed out by harshness. For this reason we have also borne the blows of words, so that we may be able at least little by little to imitate him who deigned to humble himself for our sake, and through this stroke may avoid the words of that final vengeance. Let us hear, therefore, and agree with the orator of the Church, who through the tongue of the Holy Spirit cries out with a clear voice, saying: Let all things among you be done in charity (I Corinthians XVI). So whether we inquire, or only speak, and are only heard, let charity intervene. Let some art exist for the composing and joining of good concord. For if until now we have loved silence more than garrulity of words, we have thought this indeed to be well, lest by answering your writings in kind we should stir up the tinder of injury, and be judged faint-hearted by him who proclaimed that all things should be directed towards charity. Ours is the endeavour where the establishment of peace remains for those who are in the arena of piety; well is the one glory and crown given to the intercessor. We have been made manifest to God, who judges and tests all things. We do not stand contentiously, we do not look to contradiction, nor do we embrace empty favour: but we are known to have made the resolution of this inquiry by setting forth the word of God, trusting that the Lord God of peace will preserve unity and love towards one another among us in the glory of his most kindly majesty. objection.original: κατὰ τὴν ἄδηλον διαπνοὴν ἄνευ τῶν ἄλλων μᾶλλον γιγνομένην
objection.english: [evacuation] taking place more through the imperceptible transpiration than through the others
objection.explain: Means 'especially when imperceptible transpiration occurs without the other evacuations'; 'without' is changed into a comparison of amounts.

fixed.work: De Humero iis Modis Prolapso quos Hippocrates non Vidit
fixed.author: Galen
fixed.before: Those who have become thin from taking insufficient food because of famine or siege or mourning or grief or loss of appetite do not at once have their flesh become dry, as do those properly reduced by starving through the art. Rather, he has said that in all such circumstances they make it on the whole moister, since certain colliquations occur in it because of the deficiency. And those to whom grief is added are wasted even more; indeed the poets call griefs *meledones* [cares], as if eating and devouring the limbs (*melē*). In these all the fat is wasted away, and all the flesh that is soft and newly formed. But when a physician deliberately makes some body leaner, he does this by methods that have been found, and after this he rubs when necessary. If any colliquation should arise, [he should] evacuate it, either perceptibly through sweats or, as seen by reason, through the transpiration imperceptible to sense. And it is likely, surely, that he does not neglect foods and drinks either, but tries by these too to make all the excretions free-flowing, not only those through the belly but also those that take place through the urine. For in this way, if there were any moisture in the body due to colliquation, he would most effectively bring about its evacuation from every side out of the body. For if it remains within, it makes the flesh somewhat mucous in time, [evacuation] taking place more through the imperceptible transpiration than through the others. For whatever in the colliquations is entirely thin and serous departs and is dispersed; but the somewhat thicker part alone remains, and this, taking on a certain stickiness with time alone, becomes like mucus.

So I say briefly to your Charity; I address the Church of God, I address the people of God: if he believed, you have found [him]; if he was afraid, you have won. The Apostle says: 'Receive him who is weak in faith, not in judgements of thoughts' (Rom. 14:1). Look at the inner face, in which you may rejoice; commit the heart to God, and pray for it. Let him feel himself abandoned by the wicked, welcomed by you. Love the man more than you formerly hated the error. So Christ came to heal the sick, as we heard from the Gospel: 'For it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill' (Matt. 9:12). 'And what man is there who, when he has lost one sheep, does not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains, and go to look for the one that was lost, and when he has found it rejoices over it? So my Father rejoices over one who repents, rather than over ninety-nine righteous who have no need of repentance' (ibid. 18:12-14, and Luke 15:4-7). Precisely so Christ came to heal the sick; so he knows how to take merciful vengeance on his enemies. Those who shared his error, whose minds perhaps are grieved, are angry for the moment; afterwards perhaps they will imitate [him]. So, brothers, we commend him to your prayers, and to your love, and to your most faithful friendship, and to your taking up of his weakness. As you go before, so he follows: teach the good way, let him find it good in you. Now that he has become a Christian, let him discern what difference there is between what he has left and what he has found. Later times will prove his life and his zeal for the faith of Christ: but now, my brothers, it was not necessary, it was not the counsel of shepherds, to drive away one who was knocking, to put off one who was seeking. To want to judge the hidden things of the heart and not to accept an open declaration was neither [our] counsel nor our purpose. For we know how that merciful avarice of God threatens, as he seeks profit from his money everywhere, and says to the lazy servant who wanted to judge what he did not see, and was sluggish about gathering profit for his Lord: 'Wicked servant, out of your own mouth I condemn you. You said I was a hard man, reaping where I did not sow, gathering where I did not scatter: so you knew my avarice. You should have given my money to the money-changers, and on coming I would have demanded it with interest' (Luke 19:22-23). So we could do nothing but pay out the Lord's money. He will be the one who exacts, not of him only, but of all of us. Let us therefore fulfil the office of the dispenser, and not usurp the place of the exactor. So, my brothers, keep in mind the work of God: you were seeking one thing, planning another, and found another. We commend the Lord's work, servants to fellow servants. Let us love in him what our Lord has done more than what we wanted to do. For his works are better. And we heard his great and devout declaration: 'I do not want high office, I want to be a Christian.' Be glad, exult, love more than you hated. Commend his work to Christ in your prayers: show a faithful, devoted, friendly spirit to an old man's first lessons. For what does it matter that you see him already advanced in age? He came to the vineyard at the ninth hour, to receive an equal wage, etc.

objection.original: Si ab hominibus non toteratur injuria
objection.english: If an insult is not tolerated from men
objection.explain: Ab hominibus identifies those tolerating the insult: 'If an insult is not tolerated by human beings.' The argument compares human and divine tolerance, not the source of the insult.

fixed.author: Fulgentius Ruspensis Episcopus
fixed.before: Objection 8. Let men who desire to follow saving precepts take note that it is a crime and very blasphemous: for falsity of profession will never be able to profit those who seek to worship or venerate God by insulting [him] through blasphemy. If an insult is not tolerated from men, how could it be tolerated by the Lord, the author himself? For he shows his rebuke towards unbelievers, saying: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me (Isa. 29:13).

objection.original: ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τότε καίεσθαι τῷ σώματι, καθάπερ ζέοντι, πνευματοῦσθαί τε καὶ χεῖσθαι
objection.english: then too the body must be burned, as if boiling, and be filled with pneuma and diffused
objection.explain: The subject remains the blood; 'the body' is dative. The blood must be heated by the boiling body, become vaporous, and expand, not the body itself.

fixed.author: Galen
fixed.before: Leaving aside, then, for the present the dispute with the Empiricists, I return again to the Rationalists, examining each of the symptoms they have written down. For some of them belong to fullness relative to the faculty, some to fullness in respect of the contents, some are signs not of fullness simply but of a particular kind of fullness, and some of no fullness at all, but either of bad humours and corruption, or of a weak faculty, or of a swelling of the solid bodies. That this is so, you will learn if you pay attention to what is about to be said. The tensive condition, then, when it occurs without exercise, indicates in every case that much substance is contained in a sensitive body, but it does not further indicate what the substance is, or its kind, at least by this alone, the being stretched, which is common to every substance, thin and thick and intermediate in consistency, and pneumatic, and further hot and cold, or intermediate; rather it needs some other distinguishing marks for determining this. Lack of tone in the activities shows that the faculty is weaker, by holding back what moves, as in a weak movement of the hands; for it follows many states. For if in someone the fleshy and fatty kind should increase, while the faculty remains within the same limits, the movements must become less vigorous, since what moves stays equal while what is moved has increased; or if some one of the humours, or even all of them together, should become excessive, without the faculty increasing along with them, then too the activities must become less vigorous; or if both should increase together, the so-called parenchymata and the fluids, but the faculty does not increase with them, or if, these remaining as they were, the faculty becomes weaker. It could also happen sometimes that both come together, so that the faculty becomes weaker and the humours together with the parenchymata are either more or less, or whichever one of them; the activities become less vigorous for these reasons too, whether each of them occurs singly, or two, or more, or all together. For to think that a less vigorous movement could ever be produced by the good nourishment of the solid bodies belongs to men who do not know that the faculties pervade the solid bodies throughout, but who make the arteries and the nerves like pipes or channels for pneuma. You will know the badness of this opinion from many other [works], but not least from two treatises of ours, the one On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and the one On the Natural Faculties. Good nourishment of the solid bodies, then, is proper to good condition, while increase of the flesh is proper to good flesh and to excess of flesh. For the most part, then, the fat increases in proportion, more [than the flesh], but sometimes in fat [people] the flesh more, or the fat alone. These matters have been discussed in the commentaries On Temperaments. And just as in flesh one thing is good flesh and another excess of flesh, in the same way in blood one thing is a sort of good blood, the other excess of blood. Now it is not unclear that the state of good blood is exactly according to nature in both quality and quantity; while that of excess of blood is blameless in quality, but not blameless in quantity, but in every case more, either than what was natural from birth, or than what is relative to the faculty. For it is possible sometimes for both to increase together, beyond the nature from birth, the strength of the faculty and the quantity of the blood, as in athletic good condition; for in these the fluids and the fleshy parts and the faculty increase together in proportion to one another. And so it is now quite plain that those who called swelling of the body one of the plethoric signs do not speak truly either; for swelling of the veins would be a plethoric sign, but swelling of flesh and fat would be a fullness of those things themselves, not, however, that which we are now seeking, which is also called plethora. For having proposed to speak about this fullness, which evidently indicates evacuation, some of them went astray so far, [misled by] what is at times indicated by homonymies, as to be carried off to the fullness of flesh and fat. So bad a mark of fullness, then, is swelling of the body; for it would indicate the filling of those very veins that we see, but not necessarily of those in the depth; rather it is possible sometimes that, while the outer veins are distended, the inner ones are not distended in the same way; for example, when cold has taken hold, the blood is driven into the depth, and the outer [veins] are so drained of blood that they do not even appear; and again when there is warmth, or after bathing, the blood is carried to the skin and the outer parts of the body, leaving the depth; and if there is also a burning fever, then too the body must be burned, as if boiling, and be filled with pneuma and diffused. So swelling of the veins is not an inseparable mark of a quantity of humours, but first the body must be in such a state that neither the inner parts exceed the outer in heat nor these the inner; and second, that there is no immoderate heat in the whole animal. With these distinctions made beforehand, swelling of the veins might be a sign of the fullness now called sanguine, [so called] by predominance; for it is impossible that blood so pure should ever be contained in the veins that nothing of bile, or phlegm, or serous fluid is carried along with it, which is why earlier too I asked that it be understood in the same way whether I said that the humours were in excess or the blood. For since blood unmixed and pure of the other fluids is never contained in the veins (this has been shown by us elsewhere), but mixed blood, mixed not at random but with the others mingled with it in a certain proportion in animals in a natural state, it will make no difference whether we call it humours or blood. For when all increase together, in the natural proportion, with the blood that predominates, the name humours signifies the same thing, and it makes no difference whether we say the humours or the blood have increased, since the statement that says humours indicates just this, that there is an excess while the original proportion is wholly kept. Let this, then, be distinguished thus by us, and let us go back again to the matter in hand. Swelling of the veins, if it has arisen neither through predominance of the external state nor through diffusion and boiling, indicates that the fullness is sanguine. But such a part must also not be positioned hanging downward, or have been moved recently more than the others; therefore one might, gathering all the particular distinctions in one statement, say that swelling of the veins indicates a quantity of blood when all the parts have the same state together with moderate warmth; since if all were in the same condition but there were immoderate heat, there arises in this case a diffusion of the humours that raises the veins into swelling, which indicates a fullness not sanguine but pneumatic; for the humours become pneumatic when heated. Therefore those too who declared that swelling of the veins signifies fullness will seem to have spoken correctly, if one understands in the statement 'in those veins', in which this happens to occur; for the substance that has produced the swelling in the veins is necessarily more than before, but it is not yet clear what kind the fullness is; for unnatural swelling is common to every abundant substance, whether it is pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic.

For to think that a less vigorous movement could ever be produced by the good nourishment of the solid bodies belongs to men who do not know that the faculties pervade the solid bodies throughout, but who make the arteries and the nerves like pipes or channels for pneuma. You will know the badness of this opinion from many other [works], but not least from two treatises of ours, the one On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and the one On the Natural Faculties. Good nourishment of the solid bodies, then, is proper to good condition, while increase of the flesh is proper to good flesh and to excess of flesh. For the most part, then, the fat increases in proportion, more [than the flesh], but sometimes in fat [people] the flesh more, or the fat alone. These matters have been discussed in the commentaries On Temperaments. And just as in flesh one thing is good flesh and another excess of flesh, in the same way in blood one thing is a sort of good blood, the other excess of blood. Now it is not unclear that the state of good blood is exactly according to nature in both quality and quantity; while that of excess of blood is blameless in quality, but not blameless in quantity, but in every case more, either than what was natural from birth, or than what is relative to the faculty. For it is possible sometimes for both to increase together, beyond the nature from birth, the strength of the faculty and the quantity of the blood, as in athletic good condition; for in these the fluids and the fleshy parts and the faculty increase together in proportion to one another. And so it is now quite plain that those who called swelling of the body one of the plethoric signs do not speak truly either; for swelling of the veins would be a plethoric sign, but swelling of flesh and fat would be a fullness of those things themselves, not, however, that which we are now seeking, which is also called plethora. For having proposed to speak about this fullness, which evidently indicates evacuation, some of them went astray so far, [misled by] what is at times indicated by homonymies, as to be carried off to the fullness of flesh and fat. So bad a mark of fullness, then, is swelling of the body; for it would indicate the filling of those very veins that we see, but not necessarily of those in the depth; rather it is possible sometimes that, while the outer veins are distended, the inner ones are not distended in the same way; for example, when cold has taken hold, the blood is driven into the depth, and the outer [veins] are so drained of blood that they do not even appear; and again when there is warmth, or after bathing, the blood is carried to the skin and the outer parts of the body, leaving the depth; and if there is also a burning fever, then too the blood must be heated by the body, boiling as it is, and become vaporous and expand. So swelling of the veins is not an inseparable mark of a quantity of humours, but first the body must be in such a state that neither the inner parts exceed the outer in heat nor these the inner; and second, that there is no immoderate heat in the whole animal. With these distinctions made beforehand, swelling of the veins might be a sign of the fullness now called sanguine, [so called] by predominance; for it is impossible that blood so pure should ever be contained in the veins that nothing of bile, or phlegm, or serous fluid is carried along with it, which is why earlier too I asked that it be understood in the same way whether I said that the humours were in excess or the blood. For since blood unmixed and pure of the other fluids is never contained in the veins (this has been shown by us elsewhere), but mixed blood, mixed not at random but with the others mingled with it in a certain proportion in animals in a natural state, it will make no difference whether we call it humours or blood. For when all increase together, in the natural proportion, with the blood that predominates, the name humours signifies the same thing, and it makes no difference whether we say the humours or the blood have increased, since the statement that says humours indicates just this, that there is an excess while the original proportion is wholly kept. Let this, then, be distinguished thus by us, and let us go back again to the matter in hand. Swelling of the veins, if it has arisen neither through predominance of the external state nor through diffusion and boiling, indicates that the fullness is sanguine. But such a part must also not be positioned hanging downward, or have been moved recently more than the others; therefore one might, gathering all the particular distinctions in one statement, say that swelling of the veins indicates a quantity of blood when all the parts have the same state together with moderate warmth; since if all were in the same condition but there were immoderate heat, there arises in this case a diffusion of the humours that raises the veins into swelling, which indicates a fullness not sanguine but pneumatic; for the humours become pneumatic when heated. Therefore those too who declared that swelling of the veins signifies fullness will seem to have spoken correctly, if one understands in the statement 'in those veins', in which this happens to occur; for the substance that has produced the swelling in the veins is necessarily more than before, but it is not yet clear what kind the fullness is; for unnatural swelling is common to every abundant substance, whether it is pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic.
fixed.reason: τῷ σώματι is dative and the subject is still the blood: in a burning fever the blood is heated by the body, becomes vaporous and expands, which is why the veins swell. The English made the body the subject and lost the step the conclusion rests on.

objection.original: in frumento uero et uino et oleo, quod audiet
objection.english: in the grain and wine and oil, which it will hear
objection.explain: [10–11] The point is that he will hear through these elements, as 'qui in his sit auditurus' explains; render 'As for his hearing in the grain, wine and oil,' not 'which it will hear'.

fixed.after: But as for His hearing in the grain and wine and oil, although these insen-
fixed.reason: quod audiet is 'as for his hearing': the grain, wine and oil cannot hear, so it is he who hears in them, as the rest of the sentence says. The rest of the sentence carried the point, so minor.

objection.original: et cum omnibus iniquis me esse non denegem nequiorem
objection.english: and how shall I not deny that I am more wicked than all the wicked
objection.explain: Read 'since I do not deny that I am more wicked than all the wicked'; the English instead asks how he can refrain from denying it.

objection.original: obduratus in clementia
objection.english: hardened in clemency
objection.explain: Read 'hardened by mercilessness': in clementia is an apparent OCR split of inclementia ('cruelty'), reversing the sense when rendered as clemency.

fixed.before: 30. For if you did not refuse to the unrepentant and tearless legion of demons the herd of swine it asked for, how much more readily will you be prompt to grant pardon of sins to a faithful soul imploring you with weeping? Trusting in this, I offer you the prayers and tears of my penitence: you will save me just as [you save] the others who repent of having failed. Or will the trust and promise of your kindness and pardon, through which all the converted families of the earth are saved, remain unfruitful in my case, or become dry and void in me alone? Will your great clemency, which can never be lessened by giving, nor is constrained by the effect of any want, become insufficient in one penitent? Will you hold yourself back in me alone, so as not to bestow what is asked, made barren of the fruit of mercy? Will you be grieved against me for ever, for a sin of a short time, which, by the disposing of your providence, I repent of, cursing and abhorring it, since I am a creature from earth and ashes, corruptible and mortal, but you are God the creator, incorruptible and immortal? Will you, hardened in clemency, not hear one contrite and humbled, or will you judge it right to punish one who confesses to you, or decide to destroy one who entreats you? I shall not believe so, nor suspect that you wish it, for this is impious and against the nature of divine kindness. Therefore, suppliant and confident, I implore your mercy, that you may fulfil my petitions with kindly will.

objection.original: quae totam prorsus causam tuam consu- mit, tamquam ad validissimum stipitem alligandum
objection.english: [lies] the whole of your case, as if tied to a very strong stake
objection.explain: The Latin says that mortality completely destroys his case; alligandum refers to the male addressee, who must be tied to the stake, not to the feminine causam ('case').

fixed.author: Marius Mercator
fixed.before: 14. Nor will you have cause to laugh at the great brevity of this little work of ours, since you ought not to boast of your so numerous books, full of rough loquacity rather than of any matters worthy even of consideration. I do not want you to feign ignorance on this point; for you know that in this question which is debated between us, namely on the mortality of the human race, which through the first transgressors of the divine command has run, and runs, and will run on to the end, universally through the seeds, [lies] the whole of your case, as if tied to a very strong stake: and if the Christian and prudent reader observes that this case between us, or rather in you, has been extinguished, he will recognise that nothing, absolutely nothing further, has remained to you on which you either ought to have muttered or ought now to mutter; and he will judge that concerning your whole discourse, which you boast to be the height of eloquence, that saying fits and suits you better than the man of whom it was said: "Enough eloquence, too little wisdom. His vast mind always desired the immoderate, the incredible, the too lofty." And concerning your ideas, by which you are lifted up, wandering and vain, the prudent reader will pronounce through the mouth of another age, and will apply everywhere this saying: that the mountains were in labour with you, and from them a ridiculous mouse was born.

objection.original: τι καὶ ὑπεκφέροι τῶν λυπησάντων ἂν, εἰ μὴ ἀπέρχοιτο
objection.english: it may also carry off something of what was causing trouble, if it did not pass
objection.explain: It carries off material that would cause trouble if not discharged; the Greek describes hypothetical harm from retention, not harm already occurring.

fixed.author: Rufus of Ephesus
fixed.before: For just as in other matters season and age, constitution of the body and regimen make a great difference, both for bad and for good, so one must also form expectations about the urine; for black urine is less dangerous for an old man, in autumn and winter, and for [anyone who] is of black humours; besides, it may also carry off something of what was causing trouble, if it did not pass; but for a young man, in spring, and for anyone of moister humours, it is more serious.
fixed.after: For just as in other matters season and age, constitution of the body and regimen make a great difference, both for bad and for good, so one must also form expectations about the urine; for black urine is less dangerous for an old man, in autumn and winter, and for [anyone who] is of black humours; besides, it may also carry off something that would cause trouble if it did not pass; but for a young man, in spring, and for anyone of moister humours, it is more serious.
fixed.reason: λυπησάντων ἄν is potential: black urine may carry off matter that would cause trouble if it were not passed.

objection.original: non ut perderent, sed ut discerent reuerentiam
objection.english: not that they might ruin them but that they might learn reverence
objection.explain: [1] Reverentiam supplies the object of both verbs: the women followed 'not to lose reverence, but to learn it,' not to ruin the apostles.

noted.note: In 5, 'not that they might ruin them but that they might learn reverence' may also be read with reverentiam governing both verbs: 'not to lose reverence but to learn it'.
noted.reason: Both readings are defensible: perderent can take reverentiam with discerent, or stand alone as 'ruin [them]', which suits a treatise warning clerics against women's company.

objection.original: nihil interest quam jus atque vts
objection.english: nothing differs so much as law and force
objection.explain: The only distinction is law versus force: nihil ... quam means 'nothing except', not 'nothing so much as'.

not_upheld.reason: Cicero's own text (Pro Sestio 92) reads nihil tam interest quam ius atque vis, which the English renders; on either reading the one difference named is law against force.

objection.original: ut eripias me sica flagello temporali
objection.english: rescue me thus by a temporal scourge
objection.explain: Read sic a: 'rescue me thus from the temporal scourge'; the scourge is what he asks to escape, not the means of rescue.

not_upheld.work: ORATIO PRO CURREPTIUNE VITÆ. FLENDA SEMPER PECCATA (Appendix XVIII)
not_upheld.reason: The prayer asks to be purged here, in this life (hic ... deterge), so that nothing is left to punish in the future; 'rescue me thus by a temporal scourge' fits that, and the a after sic may be a stray footnote letter, as elsewhere in Migne's text.
